reason: The learning objective is a numerical inference: turn counts into the share of positives that are truly ill, and see that this share moves with the base rate. The evidence is the counts themselves - 9 of 59, then 99 of 149 - and text in a SceneSpec is static, so a scene could only render proportions as lengths and could not print the numbers that carry the argument. Animated areas also invite the very comparison the misconception exploits, since a bigger red patch looks more likely, and a single animated prevalence dramatises one base rate instead of letting the learner run the two-case comparison that actually changes the belief. The work the learner has to do is fill in the arithmetic at a second prevalence and compare the rows; that happens on paper, with the numbers visible and stable, not in motion.
staticAlternative: One page of natural frequencies, no animation. A 1,000 person tree at 1% prevalence: 10 ill, of whom 9 test positive at 90% sensitivity, and 990 well, of whom 50 test positive at 95% specificity, with every branch labelled by its count; beside it the box 'all positives = 59' and the box 'truly ill among the positives = 9, about 15%'. Directly underneath, the same tree for 10% prevalence with the count boxes left empty - ill ___, true positives ___, false positives ___, positives ___, share ___% - so the learner fills them in (100, 90, 45, 135, 67%) and then answers two questions: which number changed most between the rows, and did the test itself get better? A margin note does the arithmetic for the '99% accurate' claim: at 1% prevalence even a 99% sensitive test gives about 10 true positives against 50 false ones, so no single positive result settles anything. The page ends with the warning that this is arithmetic for understanding, not medical advice.
